extracted.intended_audience: political leaders, framers, and educated readers interested in constitution-making (late-18th-century America)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for creating stable republican governments: how to found, structure, and reform constitutions drawing on reason, experience, and historical models. Focuses on separation of powers, representation, practical scale, and gradual improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found governments on reason and the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments ought to be erected on the simple principles of nature; contrived merely by the use of reason and the senses rather than by miracle, superstition, or priestly/magical pretences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artifice, imposture, hypocrisy, and superstition; legitimacy should rest on reason, morality, and religion without invoking 'holy oil' or other mystic rites. (Verbatim guidance: 'governments were contrived merely by the use of reason and the senses' and 'the people universally were too enlightened to be imposed on by artifice').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult authoritative writings and practical models
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating new systems of laws and constitutions, examine celebrated works and buildings, consult writers of reputation, and compare theories with actual models to determine what is founded in nature or created by fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt advantages and reject inconveniences of prior models 'as far as their circumstances would allow.' (Analogy used: a wise architect consulting Vitruvius, Palladio, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin right because constitutions are long-lasting experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional systems are experiments affecting human life and manners that, once begun, run over whole quarters of the globe and persist for many thousands of years; therefore initial choices are of last importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because political experiments cannot be made in a laboratory or quickly reversed, framers must take care to 'begin right'; if set out wrong they may never return to the right path except by accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers into distinct branches (threefold division)
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic should have distinct divisions of power — a governor (executive), a senate (aristocratical branch), and a house of representatives (democratical branch) — to measure and secure justice over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero and Tacitus' authority favors three branches: 'the laws...can be safe of protection in no other form of government,' and skillful arrangement (like musical parts by Handel) produces harmony; confused mixture produces destructive cacophony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the people's property and interests in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The very name of a republic implies that the property of the people should be represented in the legislature and the rule of justice decided there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited monarchy with two independent branches may be called a republic if it is a government of laws and the legislature represents the people's property and secures justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating all authority in an impractical 'nation-as-centre' direct democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting all authority into 'one centre' — the nation voting as a whole on every matter — is impractical and unintelligible for extensive populations and territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure democracy (whole-population assemblies) is feasible only at very small scale (e.g., a village); for large states like Virginia it is unworkable due to logistics and time. Representative majorities/assemblies are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix sovereign authorities confusedly in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining the authority of the one (king), the few (nobles), and the many (people) confusedly in one assembly produces confusion and eventual misgovernment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (ancient Germans, assemblies of king[n] nobles and commons together) show each part claiming sovereignty, producing turbulence, wars, and revolutions; avoid conflating separate estates into a single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt institutions to local habits and customs when wise
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention of familiar customs (e.g., English customs) can be a legitimate motive for preserving particular constitutional forms if they secure liberty, property, and safety better than alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If customs are wise and good, changing them merely because of animus against a former ruler is unwise; consider whether inherited institutions actually protect people's rights before rejecting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from historical experiments and comparative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the history and institutions of other peoples (Romans, Greeks, Germans, Indians, English) as political experiments whose consequences (spread, duration, miseries) offer lessons for constitution design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wide historical reading (Hume, Gibbon, Robertson, etc.) and assess which elements spread or endured; the Teutonic institutions' long duration is cited as strong support for mixing powers rather than conflating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor gradual, educational reform over abrupt upheaval
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people aim at institutional change, it should be by gentle means and gradual advances through improvements in general education and informing the public mind rather than sudden revolutionary measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid attempts to reach more democratic ends may 'defeat themselves'; political improvements should be incremental and accompanied by public enlightenment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale constitutional forms to population and territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose forms of government appropriate to the number of people and geographic spread; forms that work for small communities (direct democracy) do not scale to large, populous territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical governance requires representative mechanisms, moderators, clerks, committees, and delegated officers (moderator as effective leader in small assemblies but inappropriate as sole solution for large polities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design the arrangement of branches to produce harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The three branches must be arranged with skill and order so that their interaction produces concord and security rather than discord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to musical composition: properly arranged treble, tenor, and bass produce rapture; if confused together they 'rend with tremendous sound asunder.' Ensure institutional checks are orderly and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground authority in moral and reasonable foundations rather than divine privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority in magistrates and obedience of citizens can be grounded on reason, morality, and Christianity without recourse to monastic priesthoods or political knavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thirteen governments founded on natural authority of the people show the experiment succeeded; legitimacy based on reason and morals is sufficient and preferable to claims of miraculous sanction.
